memoryTip: Amalgam = mix (like dental amalgam) — combine.
correctPassage: The two departments will amalgamate next year under a single chair.
wrongPassages: They tried to amalgamate the floodplain risk by rebranding it “riverfront charm.”
She hoped to amalgamate the walkout by requiring smiling photos for the intranet.
She tried to amalgamate the bias by surveying only people who already agreed.

memoryTip: Pro-mulgate: broadcast the rule widely.
correctPassage: Agencies must promulgate new rules before they can enforce them.
wrongPassages: They meant to promulgate surplus by producing more of the model nobody bought.
They hoped to promulgate the protest by scheduling the vote for 5 a.m.
The cleaner will promulgate the spill by pushing it toward the floor drain.

definition: the practice of exchanging things for mutual benefit
memoryTip: Reciprocal giving — you scratch my back…
correctPassage: Trade talks stalled over the principle of reciprocity.
wrongPassages: She burned reciprocity onto a drum that held only packing peanuts.
The sack chalked reciprocity held receipts from closed stores only.
The dumpster was repainted and the Reciprocity Point sign was removed.

memoryTip: En-tail: necessarily brings along X as a consequence.
correctPassage: Accepting the grant will entail detailed quarterly reporting.
wrongPassages: His entail confidence vanished as soon as the first hard question was asked.
The bass line was entail and never locked with the kick drum.
The station’s entail platform screen showed yesterday’s departures all day.

definition: demand or specify as part of an agreement
memoryTip: Stipulate terms — specify as a condition.
correctPassage: The contract stipulates that all data remain open for five years.
wrongPassages: The runner will stipulate the failure by swallowing exceptions and returning success.
He moved to stipulate the deposition by answering only with prepared slogans.
She tried to stipulate the fever by withholding treatment until overnight hours.

memoryTip: Like an emblem — symbolic of a bigger idea.
correctPassage: The ruined factory became emblematic of the region’s industrial decline.
wrongPassages: The wharf looked emblematic at slack tide with a clear open horizon.
Investors wanted emblematic markets so prices would never move more than a cent.
The mudflat stayed emblematic in a tide model locked permanently at low water.

memoryTip: A-bate: lessen — reduction (noise abatement).
correctPassage: Noise abatement measures reduced complaints from nearby residents.
wrongPassages: City hall issued an abatement that only certified the applicant’s shoe size.
She bought “Abatement Sand” paint, a standard beige in every hardware aisle.
The bag tagged abatement held lanyards and a sticky opener.

memoryTip: Dis-sonance: harsh sound / clash of ideas.
correctPassage: There is cognitive dissonance between the company’s values and its practices.
wrongPassages: She pointed “see dissonance” at a coffee ring and closed the style guide.
The monitor sticky dissonance yellowed and never gained a task.
The tote tagged dissonance held spare badges and a dead radio.

memoryTip: Cut the tail short — reduce or cut short.
correctPassage: Budget cuts will curtail after-school programs this semester.
wrongPassages: The bay looked curtail under foghorns with no hulls visible on the water.
The board’s curtail minutes recorded motions, votes, and abstentions in order.
His curtail certificate of conference claimed talks that never took place.

memoryTip: Fort + attitude — courage under hardship.
correctPassage: Survivors showed remarkable fortitude in the months after the disaster.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the methods fortitude once every step could be repeated elsewhere.
His fortitude proposed order left the relief section completely blank.
The ice lip felt fortitude on a grated overlook with warning signs.

memoryTip: Stern face / ship’s stern — serious and strict.
correctPassage: The judge’s stern warning made clear that further violations would not be tolerated.
wrongPassages: He ranked the obstacle stern after walking around it in ten seconds.
The crevasse hop felt stern on a seasonal bridge with rails.
He greened the PIR checklist as stern with owners still unassigned.

memoryTip: Like a prophet — predicts what’s coming.
correctPassage: Her early essay now seems prophetic in light of later events.
wrongPassages: a prophetic integration test mocks every dependency, including the system under test.
Her prophetic sketch caught the likeness in a few decisive lines.
Critics called the clean version prophetic for removing the song’s only edge.

memoryTip: De-cry: cry against publicly — denounce.
correctPassage: Local historians decry the demolition of the old theater.
wrongPassages: Parents called the concert decry after every child sat still through two full hours.
Her decry printer’s note described a binding that was never used.
The ice tongue tip felt decry behind a fence and viewing platform.

memoryTip: Flip answers — unserious, disrespectful levity.
correctPassage: Flippancy about safety rules has no place in a laboratory.
wrongPassages: She kept a spare flippancy in the desk drawer among rubber bands.
The butt chalked flippancy held spare gaskets and a blunt pencil.
The carton marked flippancy held only void-fill and a packing slip.

memoryTip: Full of quirks — oddly charming peculiarities.
correctPassage: The building’s quirky layout reflects its history as a series of additions.
wrongPassages: The leading-tone held was quirky under a final open fifth on I.
The wharf’s quirky bollard load plate was for gear never installed on site.
The approach felt quirky on a catwalk with welded railings.

definition: courtesy and considerate behavior among people or nations
memoryTip: Committee of courtesy — mutual respect among groups.
correctPassage: Diplomatic comity requires that each side treat the other with basic respect.
wrongPassages: The empty bullet comity stayed empty through three revisions.
The firkin branded comity held wristbands still linked together.
The form field comity accepted any string and never validated it.

definition: having a sharp or critical quality
memoryTip: Mord- = bite — sharp, biting wit.
correctPassage: Her mordant wit left few illusions about the proposal’s weaknesses.
wrongPassages: The stand looked mordant in rain with awnings still rolled up.
The trail was so mordant that first-time hikers finished early without maps or guides.
The cattle dock looked mordant with ramps chained and unused for years.

memoryTip: Onus = burden — heavy, burdensome duty.
correctPassage: The reporting requirements proved onerous for small nonprofits.
wrongPassages: The clinic tried to onerous no-shows by double-booking every appointment slot.
The explosion hatch was onerous and never opened in the overpressure test.
The queue tried to onerous ASA by answering and parking callers on mute.

definition: an attempt to make something that is not the case appear true
memoryTip: Pretend-sense — fake appearance of something.
correctPassage: Under the pretense of routine maintenance, the system was quietly redesigned.
wrongPassages: The trail felt pretense under boardwalk that never touched the mud.
The thermal fuse was pretense and never opened in the oven test.
The countersubject was pretense and never entered stretto.

definition: given to sudden changes of mood; unpredictable
memoryTip: Like a goat’s caper (capra) — sudden mood jumps.
correctPassage: Capricious enforcement of the rules undermined trust in the process.
wrongPassages: The crowd noise was capricious after the engineer isolated a single clap.
She treated the requirement as capricious after the client waived it in writing.
He marked maintenance capricious while the change window still ran long.
